claims.text: In HEAs outside Nb–Ta and titanium-rich systems, superconductivity is primarily governed by the degree of local lattice distortion induced by chemical disorder.
Local lattice distortions modify the phonon spectrum.
Changes in the phonon spectrum modulate electron–phonon coupling strength.
Electron–phonon coupling strength sets the superconducting transition temperature.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes induce local lattice strain and deviations from perfect crystallinity.
Increasing the average variance in constituent atomic radii increases local lattice distortion.
Atomic-size-induced lattice distortion causes phonon softening.
Greater local distortion enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling increases pairing strength.
Increased pairing strength raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Samples with greater atomic-radius variance and measured lattice distortion will have a higher Tc than a low-size-dispersion baseline HEA.
There is an optimal distortion level beyond which detrimental scattering may counteract the superconducting benefit.
Identical annealing conditions can isolate the effect of atomic-radius variance across compositionally different samples.
Annealing in argon at 800–1000°C for a fixed time will produce homogeneous, equilibrated samples.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to single-phase, fully miscible solid-solution HEAs and may fail in segregated, ordered, or multiphase materials.
A lack of Tc enhancement in samples with increased atomic-size variance and measured distortion would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows Tc enhancement to disappear beyond an unspecified optimal distortion because of detrimental scattering, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of any higher-distortion sample to enhance Tc as falsifying. Without defining the optimal range, an adverse result can be explained by the stated caveat rather than decisively falsifying the mechanism.
